screens.title: Initial Configuration and System Management
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll walk through the essential steps you perform when you first bring up a Juniper device. You will learn how to give the device a clear hostname so it is easy to identify, how to secure administrative access by setting root and non-root user accounts, and how Junos protects you with a candidate configuration model that requires a commit to activate changes. We'll also show the safety features you should rely on: commit check to validate syntax, commit confirmed to provide an automatic rollback timer when you make risky remote changes, and rollback to recover a previous working state if something goes wrong. Finally, you'll see how to configure a simple interface with an IPv4 address so the device can communicate on the network. These steps are small individually but together they form the foundation of a stable, auditable device configuration process. As you go through the hands-on activity later, think about how each command reduces risk: naming improves clarity, separate accounts reduce exposure, and commit workflows protect continuity. How might you apply these rules in your lab or production environment to avoid a simple mistake becoming a costly outage?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Initial Configuration
Initial Configuration and System Management
Secure device identity, admin access, and interface connectivity using Junos configuration workflows.
This chapter introduces the commands and habits you need to set a hostname, secure the root account, create administrative users with appropriate privileges, validate and commit changes safely, and configure an interface. These practices reduce downtime and help you recover quickly from mistakes.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson
Device Identity
Set a hostname so devices are easy to identify across a network of routers.
Coming up
Admin Access
Protect root and use named accounts with least privilege for day-to-day tasks.
Also
Safe Commit
Validate with commit check, use commit confirmed remotely, and recover with rollback.
Configuration Flow
Set Hostname
Identify the device with a unique name.
Create Users
Avoid using root for daily administration.
Commit & Rollback
Use commit check, commit confirmed, and rollback to manage risk.
Quick lab
Try these first commands
configure
set system host-name MyJNCIA-Router
set system root-authentication plain-text-password
set system login user student class super-user authentication plain-text-password
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family inet address 192.168.100.1/24
commit check
commit confirmed 5

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to perform the core setup tasks every Junos administrator must know. You will confidently name devices for clear identification, secure the root account and create named user accounts so day-to-day tasks do not rely on the unrestricted root user. You will understand the candidate-commit model: edits live in a candidate configuration until you explicitly commit them, and you'll use commit check to validate syntax before enabling changes. You will also apply commit confirmed when making risky, remote updates so the device can automatically revert if you lose access. These skills reduce human error and maintain network availability. Each objective pairs a practical command with the reason it matters in operations, so you not only type the command but also justify it during troubleshooting or change control.

screens.title: Entering Configuration Mode and Setting Hostname
screens.narratorSegment: Configuration mode is the workspace where changes are staged. When you enter with the configure command you move from operational mode to an edit session where every set and delete alters the candidate configuration, not the running system. One of the first edits you usually make is to set a hostname within the system hierarchy. A clear, descriptive hostname helps you find the device in inventories, maps, and logs. For example, set system host-name MyRouter-Branch1 to mark both function and location. A common misconception is that changing a hostname immediately alters all logs or external monitoring; in fact the change does not take effect until you commit. Another pitfall is creating inconsistent naming schemes — use a predictable pattern like site-role-number to reduce confusion. Practice: enter configure, run the set host-name command, then use show | compare to inspect the candidate changes. The compare output shows exactly what will change when you commit. Takeaway: treat configuration mode as a draft area, name devices consistently, and always review your staged edits before committing so your network remains organized and predictable. Entering Configuration Mode and Setting Hostname means set the hostname in configuration mode and review staged changes; the commit step activates the new name.. In practical terms, where you edit the candidate configuration and why a hostname matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept
Configuration Mode and Hostname
Enter the candidate configuration, stage changes, and use a consistent hostname pattern to simplify operations.
What is configuration mode?
  • It is the edit workspace where commands modify the candidate configuration.
  • Changes remain inactive until validated and committed.
  • Use show | compare to preview changes before commit.
Common mistake
Forgetting to commit after setting a hostname; the device will still present the old name until commit completes.
Key Takeaway
Make naming consistent and always review candidate changes prior to commit.
Example — CLI sequence
user@router> configure
Entering configuration mode
[edit]
user@router# set system host-name MyRouter-Branch1
[edit]
user@router# show | compare
---
+ system {
+     host-name MyRouter-Branch1;
+ }
[edit]
Try this
After staging the hostname, run show | compare and confirm the change before using commit. This prevents surprise edits.

screens.title: Setting Root Password and Protecting the Root Account
screens.narratorSegment: The root user has full unrestricted access to the device and is therefore the highest-value account to protect. Setting a strong root password is one of the first security tasks. Junos allows you to set a plain-text password that the system encrypts when you commit; the command path is set system root-authentication plain-text-password. A common misunderstanding is that you can avoid creating extra users by sharing the root password; this increases risk and obscures audit trails. Instead, create named users for day-to-day work and reserve root for emergency tasks. When you choose a password, prefer long passphrases or complex character mixes to resist guessing. Also consider central authentication for larger deployments, but for an individual device a secure local root password is essential. As an exercise, set the root password, then create a non-root administrative account and verify both can log in with the expected privileges. Takeaway: treat root as an emergency tool, lock it with a strong password, and record separate user accounts so every action is attributable. Setting Root Password and Protecting the Root Account means root is powerful; secure it and use separate user accounts to enforce accountability and limit daily exposure.. In practical terms, why the root user is sensitive and how junos stores passwords. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Protect the highest privilege
keyIdea.text: Root is powerful; secure it and use separate user accounts to enforce accountability and limit daily exposure.

content.html:
Definition
Root Password and Administrative Safety
Set a secure root password and create named administrative users instead of sharing root credentials.
Why it matters
Root can change system state, erase configs, or lock out other admins. Securing this account prevents accidental or malicious wide-impact changes.
Misconception: Sharing root is convenient. Reality: it removes accountability and increases risk.
Key Takeaway
Use strong passwords and separate accounts for daily tasks so you limit exposure and enable audit trails.
CLI example
[edit]
user@router# set system root-authentication plain-text-password
New password:
Retype new password:
[edit]
Concrete exercise
Set a strong root password, then create a user account named admin and give it the super-user class. Confirm you can authenticate with the new account before ending a session.

screens.title: Creating User Accounts and Login Classes
screens.narratorSegment: Creating named user accounts supports the principle of least privilege and improves operational hygiene. In Junos, users are defined under system login user NAME and assigned a class such as super-user for full privileges or a custom class for restricted access. When you add an account, you specify authentication and often a plain-text password that the system will encrypt on commit. The main benefit is accountability: actions are tied to a user instead of a shared root password. A practical example is creating a daily admin account with super-user class for routine maintenance while keeping root reserved for emergency tasks. A common misconception is that a super-user account is the same as root; while permissions are equivalent, using a named account preserves an audit trail. Also avoid making every admin a super-user; where possible, create narrower classes to limit exposure. After creating users, test login and verify class behavior with show system users. Takeaway: create named accounts, assign minimal privileges needed, and test access before relying on them in production. Creating User Accounts and Login Classes means define users with specific classes so daily operations are auditable and reduce reliance on the root account.. In practical terms, least privilege, login classes, and why named accounts matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
User Accounts & Login Classes
Create named accounts and assign classes to control privileges and auditing.
Steps
  1. Create user under system login.
  2. Assign a login class such as super-user for full access or a custom restricted class.
  3. Set authentication and verify login behavior.
Misconception
Thinking every admin should be a super-user; prefer restricted classes for specific tasks when possible.
Key Takeaway
Use named users for day-to-day tasks and keep root as an emergency fallback to protect your system and its audit trail.
CLI example
[edit]
user@router# set system login user admin class super-user authentication plain-text-password
New password:
Retype new password:
[edit]
user@router# commit
Scenario
Create a student account in a lab, limit its class if you want to practice safer privilege separation, and verify you can log in and run expected show commands.

screens.title: Commit Workflow: commit, commit check, and commit confirmed
screens.narratorSegment: The commit workflow is central to safe configuration management. After you stage edits in the candidate configuration, use commit check to run a syntax and basic validation without activating the changes. This catches common errors early. When you are ready to activate, commit validates again and then applies the changes to the active configuration. For remote changes that could remove your access, commit confirmed provides a safety timer: the new config is applied but will automatically revert after the specified number of minutes unless you run commit again to confirm. For example, commit confirmed 5 will revert in five minutes unless re-confirmed. A typical workflow is: edit, run commit check, run commit confirmed N when remote, test access, and then run commit to finalize. A common misconception is that commit confirmed is a substitute for careful testing; it is not—it's a safety net for accidental lockout. Always plan your test steps before committing and have rollback and console access procedures ready. Takeaway: validate before activation and use commit confirmed when you cannot be physically present to recover the device if access is lost.

keyIdea.title: Validate before you activate
keyIdea.text: Use commit check to catch errors and commit confirmed as a timed safety net for remote changes, then finalize with commit when satisfied.

content.html:
Process Flow
Commit, Commit Check, Commit Confirmed
A disciplined commit workflow prevents syntax errors and accidental lockout during remote changes.
Recommended sequence
  1. Edit candidate configuration.
  2. Run commit check to validate syntax.
  3. If remote and risky, run commit confirmed <minutes> and test access.
  4. If tests pass, run commit to finalize.
Misconception
Assuming commit confirmed replaces testing. It only reverts automatically; you still must verify functionality during the timer.
Key Takeaway
Use commit check for syntax validation and commit confirmed as a temporary safety net when making remote edits.
Command examples and scenario
[edit]
user@router# commit check
[edit]
user@router# commit confirmed 5
commit complete (will confirm in 5 minutes unless confirmed)
# test connectivity and log in as new user
user@router# commit
commit complete
Scenario: When changing management IP remotely, use commit confirmed to avoid permanent lockout if you mistype the address.

screens.title: Rollback: Recovering a Previous Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Rollback is Junos' built-in safety valve for configuration mistakes. The system keeps a history of committed configurations. When you issue rollback 0 you load the most recent committed configuration into the candidate configuration; rollback 1 loads the previous one, and so on. After loading a rollback, you must commit to make it active. This two-step approach—load then commit—gives you an opportunity to inspect the rollback before activation. Rollback is most useful when a committed change causes instability or loss of connectivity and you need to restore a known good state quickly. A common misconception is to expect rollback to instantly become active; remember it only loads into the candidate configuration until you commit. Always inspect the loaded configuration and, if possible, use a console or out-of-band path to perform the rollback if network connectivity is impaired. Takeaway: keep rollback in your recovery plan, know how to reference previous commits by index, and confirm before committing the recovered configuration. Rollback: Recovering a Previous Configuration means use rollback indexes to restore earlier committed configurations and commit to activate the recovered state.. In practical terms, how rollback works and why it's a crucial recovery tool. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Quick recovery
keyIdea.text: Use rollback indexes to restore earlier committed configurations and commit to activate the recovered state.

content.html:
Definition
Rollback and Configuration History
Rollback loads a previous committed config into candidate so you can restore a known good state after an error.
How to think about indexes
  • rollback 0 = most recent committed configuration
  • rollback 1 = the commit before that, and so on
  • After rollback, review and run commit to apply.
Misconception
Assuming rollback immediately changes running state. It only stages the prior config until you commit.
Key Takeaway
Rollback is a fast way to recover; always inspect then commit the rollback to make it active.
CLI example
[edit]
user@router# rollback 0
load complete
[edit]
user@router# show | compare
# inspect the loaded config
user@router# commit
commit complete
Scenario: After a remote change disables routing, use rollback to restore the last known good configuration and regain stability quickly.

screens.title: Interface Configuration for Basic Connectivity
screens.narratorSegment: Interfaces are how the device reaches other systems and how administrators manage it. Junos uses a hierarchical interface configuration where you select the physical port, define a unit number for logical subinterfaces, pick a family such as inet for IPv4, and then set an address. For example, set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family inet address 192.168.1.1/24 assigns an IPv4 address to the first logical unit on the physical port. A common mistake is using the wrong prefix length, which can leave hosts unreachable; double-check both the address and mask. After configuring the interface, commit the changes and verify with show interfaces terse to ensure the interface is up and the address is present. If you configure a management interface like fxp0, remember it may be used for out-of-band access—treat those addresses carefully. Takeaway: configure interface addresses deliberately, validate with show commands, and use commit check before applying changes that affect reachability. Interface Configuration for Basic Connectivity means assign addresses with unit and family, validate the prefix length, then commit and verify with show interfaces terse.. In practical terms, assigning ipv4 addresses to physical interfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interfaces enable management access
keyIdea.text: Assign addresses with unit and family, validate the prefix length, then commit and verify with show interfaces terse.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Configure a Physical Interface
Assign a logical unit and IPv4 family, then set the address and commit.
Key points
  • Use unit 0 for a basic logical interface unless you need subinterfaces.
  • family inet selects IPv4 addressing.
  • Confirm address and prefix to avoid routing errors.
Common mistake
Typos in the prefix length (for example /24 vs /16) can isolate your device from the intended network.
Key Takeaway
Configure interfaces carefully and verify connectivity immediately after commit to catch address mistakes.
CLI example
[edit]
user@router# set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family inet address 192.168.1.1/24
[edit]
user@router# commit
commit complete
user@router> show interfaces terse
Interface               Admin Link Proto    Local                 Remote
ge-0/0/0                up    up   inet     192.168.1.1/24
Scenario: Assign a management IP to ge-0/0/0 in a lab and test ping to a host in the same subnet to confirm basic connectivity.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often encounter the same set of mistakes when first configuring Junos devices. The most frequent is forgetting to commit — edits made in configuration mode remain in the candidate configuration until you explicitly commit. screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough gives you a step-by-step pattern to perform initial device setup safely. Start by entering configuration mode with configure and set the hostname with a predictable pattern. Next, set the root password and immediately create a named administrative user so you can test delegated access without relying on root. screens.title: How Candidate Configuration, Commit, and Active System Relate
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the configuration lifecycle helps you reason about safety and rollback. Junos maintains a clear separation: the candidate configuration is where you make edits; it is not live until a commit activates it. Each commit produces a new committed configuration stored in the device's history. Because commits are discrete and indexed, rollback can load a previous committed state into the candidate workspace for inspection. This model provides auditability: you can show differences between the candidate and the active configuration with show | compare, and you can examine prior commits to track what changed and when. A misconception is treating the CLI like a direct live editor; in Junos you always signal intent to apply changes with commit. Practically, this model enables safer change control: stage complex changes, validate them, and use commit confirmed when remote. Takeaway: think in drafts and snapshots—candidate edits are drafts, commits create snapshots, and rollback restores snapshots when needed. Core Concept
Candidate → Commit → Active
Treat edits as drafts and commits as snapshots to preserve auditability and enable rollback.
Lifecycle summary
  • Candidate: staged changes you edit.
  • Commit: validates and creates a new active snapshot.
  • Rollback: retrieve and load a prior snapshot into candidate.
Audit tip
Use show | compare and saved commit history to review who changed what and when during troubleshooting.

Think of commits as checkpoints; they let you return to a known state and provide a clear change history.
Concept snapshot
Example sequence to inspect differences and history:
# show | compare   # see candidate vs active
# show system commit    # list commit history
# rollback 0
# show | compare   # inspect loaded rollback
# commit

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll walk through the essential steps you perform when you first bring up a Juniper device. You will learn how to give the device a clear hostname so it is easy to identify, how to secure administrative access by setting root and non-root user accounts, and how Junos protects you with a candidate configuration model that requires a commit to activate changes. We'll also show the safety features you should rely on: commit check to validate syntax, commit confirmed to provide an automatic rollback timer when you make risky remote changes, and rollback to recover a previous working state if something goes wrong. Finally, you'll see how to configure a simple interface with an IPv4 address so the device can communicate on the network. These steps are small individually but together they form the foundation of a stable, auditable device configuration process. As you go through the hands-on activity later, think about how each command reduces risk: naming improves clarity, separate accounts reduce exposure, and commit workflows protect continuity. How might you apply these rules in your lab or production environment to avoid a simple mistake becoming a costly outage?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to perform the core setup tasks every Junos administrator must know. You will confidently name devices for clear identification, secure the root account and create named user accounts so day-to-day tasks do not rely on the unrestricted root user. You will understand the candidate-commit model: edits live in a candidate configuration until you explicitly commit them, and you'll use commit check to validate syntax before enabling changes. You will also apply commit confirmed when making risky, remote updates so the device can automatically revert if you lose access. These skills reduce human error and maintain network availability. Each objective pairs a practical command with the reason it matters in operations, so you not only type the command but also justify it during troubleshooting or change control.

This second objectives slide highlights practical judgment and safety during configuration. You'll learn when to choose root versus a named administrative account, and how assigning a named user supports auditing and a minimal attack surface. You'll be able to explain the difference between a candidate configuration and the active running configuration, so you don't accidentally assume edits have taken effect before committing. You'll also practice the rollback command to return a device to a known good state if a commit introduces a problem. Finally, you'll apply best-practice checks—such as commit check and time-limited commit confirmed—when making remote changes that could cut your access. These objectives emphasize not only the commands, but the operational decisions that protect availability and simplify troubleshooting. Learning Objectives — Continued means learning both commands and when to use them prevents mistakes, supports recovery, and makes device management predictable and auditable.. In practical terms, skills and safety practices you'll adopt. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Configuration mode is the workspace where changes are staged. When you enter with the configure command you move from operational mode to an edit session where every set and delete alters the candidate configuration, not the running system. One of the first edits you usually make is to set a hostname within the system hierarchy. A clear, descriptive hostname helps you find the device in inventories, maps, and logs. For example, set system host-name MyRouter-Branch1 to mark both function and location. A common misconception is that changing a hostname immediately alters all logs or external monitoring; in fact the change does not take effect until you commit. Another pitfall is creating inconsistent naming schemes — use a predictable pattern like site-role-number to reduce confusion. Practice: enter configure, run the set host-name command, then use show | compare to inspect the candidate changes. The compare output shows exactly what will change when you commit. Takeaway: treat configuration mode as a draft area, name devices consistently, and always review your staged edits before committing so your network remains organized and predictable. Entering Configuration Mode and Setting Hostname means set the hostname in configuration mode and review staged changes; the commit step activates the new name.. In practical terms, where you edit the candidate configuration and why a hostname matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The root user has full unrestricted access to the device and is therefore the highest-value account to protect. Setting a strong root password is one of the first security tasks. Junos allows you to set a plain-text password that the system encrypts when you commit; the command path is set system root-authentication plain-text-password. A common misunderstanding is that you can avoid creating extra users by sharing the root password; this increases risk and obscures audit trails. Instead, create named users for day-to-day work and reserve root for emergency tasks. When you choose a password, prefer long passphrases or complex character mixes to resist guessing. Also consider central authentication for larger deployments, but for an individual device a secure local root password is essential. As an exercise, set the root password, then create a non-root administrative account and verify both can log in with the expected privileges. Takeaway: treat root as an emergency tool, lock it with a strong password, and record separate user accounts so every action is attributable. Setting Root Password and Protecting the Root Account means root is powerful; secure it and use separate user accounts to enforce accountability and limit daily exposure.. In practical terms, why the root user is sensitive and how junos stores passwords. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Creating named user accounts supports the principle of least privilege and improves operational hygiene. In Junos, users are defined under system login user NAME and assigned a class such as super-user for full privileges or a custom class for restricted access. When you add an account, you specify authentication and often a plain-text password that the system will encrypt on commit. The main benefit is accountability: actions are tied to a user instead of a shared root password. A practical example is creating a daily admin account with super-user class for routine maintenance while keeping root reserved for emergency tasks. A common misconception is that a super-user account is the same as root; while permissions are equivalent, using a named account preserves an audit trail. Also avoid making every admin a super-user; where possible, create narrower classes to limit exposure. After creating users, test login and verify class behavior with show system users. Takeaway: create named accounts, assign minimal privileges needed, and test access before relying on them in production. The commit workflow is central to safe configuration management. After you stage edits in the candidate configuration, use commit check to run a syntax and basic validation without activating the changes. This catches common errors early. When you are ready to activate, commit validates again and then applies the changes to the active configuration. For remote changes that could remove your access, commit confirmed provides a safety timer: the new config is applied but will automatically revert after the specified number of minutes unless you run commit again to confirm. For example, commit confirmed 5 will revert in five minutes unless re-confirmed. A typical workflow is: edit, run commit check, run commit confirmed N when remote, test access, and then run commit to finalize. A common misconception is that commit confirmed is a substitute for careful testing; it is not—it's a safety net for accidental lockout. Always plan your test steps before committing and have rollback and console access procedures ready. Takeaway: validate before activation and use commit confirmed when you cannot be physically present to recover the device if access is lost.

Rollback is Junos' built-in safety valve for configuration mistakes. The system keeps a history of committed configurations. When you issue rollback 0 you load the most recent committed configuration into the candidate configuration; rollback 1 loads the previous one, and so on. After loading a rollback, you must commit to make it active. This two-step approach—load then commit—gives you an opportunity to inspect the rollback before activation. Rollback is most useful when a committed change causes instability or loss of connectivity and you need to restore a known good state quickly. A common misconception is to expect rollback to instantly become active; remember it only loads into the candidate configuration until you commit. Always inspect the loaded configuration and, if possible, use a console or out-of-band path to perform the rollback if network connectivity is impaired. Takeaway: keep rollback in your recovery plan, know how to reference previous commits by index, and confirm before committing the recovered configuration. Interfaces are how the device reaches other systems and how administrators manage it. Junos uses a hierarchical interface configuration where you select the physical port, define a unit number for logical subinterfaces, pick a family such as inet for IPv4, and then set an address.
